item.description: The Provo City Council unanimously approved an ordinance requiring new developments to use dark-sky-compliant outdoor lighting, joining other Utah communities working to reduce light pollution. The new standards, based on principles from the Illuminating Engineering Society and DarkSky International, require lower color-temperature bulbs, fully shielded fixtures directing light downward, and capped display brightness, applying to new installations and major remodels rather than retroactively. Provo Power director Patricio Hernandez said the utility has already been installing dark-sky-compliant streetlights in recent years, and the council said it plans to revisit the rules to address holiday and event lighting.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: Second man charged in violent 2025 West Valley burglary and assault
item.description: Prosecutors charged a second man, 32-year-old Pedro Isaac Bonilla Urbina, in a March 2025 home invasion in which two men broke into a West Valley City apartment, robbed a woman of jewelry and bank cards, and sexually assaulted her at gunpoint while her young daughter was in another room. Bonilla Urbina faces aggravated robbery, aggravated burglary, two counts of aggravated sexual assault and related charges; the first man charged, Efrain Jose Gregorio Monroy-Lara, was identified last year through the victim's stolen bank cards and a national DNA database. Prosecutors described the case in charging documents as "something out of the movies," noting the victim begged for her life and for her daughter's safety during the assault. Monroy-Lara's next court hearing is scheduled for Sept. 14.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Fire breaks out at Salt Lake City recycling center for second time in 4 months
item.description: A fire broke out at a Poplar Grove neighborhood recycling facility on Orange Street in Salt Lake City on Tuesday, the second blaze at the same METech Recycling building in four months after a May 19 fire. Salt Lake City Fire Capt. Chad Jepperson said the single-alarm fire quickly escalated to a second alarm requiring about 50 firefighters, and a small grass fire sparked by embers nearby was also extinguished. No injuries were reported and all employees evacuated safely; the building's concrete exterior kept flames from spreading inside, though officials urged nearby residents to stay indoors and close windows because of smoke from burning wood, cardboard and electronic waste. The cause remains under investigation.
item.dc:creator: Mary Culbertson and Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: He's a 'horrible, horrible human being,' mother calls her daughter's killer
item.description: Tammy Edmunds testified before the Utah Board of Pardons and Parole on Tuesday urging that Anthony Jeffrey Christensen, convicted of murdering her daughter Kammy Mae Edmunds in 2020, never be released from prison. Christensen, now 44, beat his fiancee to death in 2017 and tried to stage the killing as a drunk-driving accident, but a medical examiner found her injuries were blunt-force trauma inconsistent with a car crash. Because Christensen's scheduled parole hearing isn't until 2040, the family requested an earlier impact hearing out of concern Tammy Edmunds might not be alive by then. She described her daughter as kind and universally loved but said Christensen was "a horrible, horrible human being."
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Labor Day DUI enforcement highlights efforts to prevent impaired driving in Utah
item.description: Utah Highway Patrol and dozens of local agencies ramped up DUI patrols over Labor Day weekend as the state closed out its "100 Deadliest Days" stretch, with more than 245 extra overtime DUI shifts logged across 39 agencies statewide, per the Department of Public Safety. UHP Lt. Zach Randall said troopers suspect impairment and speeding contributed to a fatal Salt Lake County crash over the weekend and stressed that drunk driving is entirely preventable. State Rep. Steve Eliason said he's preparing legislation for the next session that would expand alcohol-purchase restrictions to more DUI offenders and could penalize bars with high rates of DUI-linked patrons, citing more than 100 annual Utah drunk-driving deaths. Randall urged drivers to arrange a sober ride before they start drinking, noting enforcement remained heightened into Monday night as the holiday wrapped up.
item.dc:creator: Emma Benson, KSL

item.title: Utahns flock to Millcreek Canyon for affordable Labor Day getaway
item.description: Cooler temperatures drew hikers, mountain bikers and picnicking families to Millcreek Canyon on Labor Day for one of the last big outdoor outings of the summer. Mountain biker Alex Khajavi said the canyon offered inexpensive recreation after a tough, hot riding season at its lower elevation. The Warnick family grilled steaks and corn at a canyon picnic site, with Brock Warnick saying Utah's outdoor access is hard to match for the price elsewhere. Parking filled quickly as crowds took advantage of the unofficial end of summer, even though the season doesn't officially end until the autumnal equinox on Sept. 22.
item.dc:creator: Annette Campbell, KSL

item.title: Salt Lake unveils markers noting 1866 lynching and a historic alternative gathering spot
item.description: Salt Lake City unveiled two new historical markers on Aug. 25 as part of a pilot program, led by Councilman Chris Wharton, meant to broaden the range of stories commemorated around the city beyond pioneer-era history. One marker, sought by the Sema Hadithi African American Heritage and Culture Foundation, memorializes Thomas Coleman, a Black man lynched in Salt Lake City in 1866 near where his body was found. The other, pursued by the Mildred Berryman Institute for LGBTIQ2S+ Utah History, honors the Sun Tavern, a bar that served as a de facto community hub for gay, lesbian and bisexual Utahns after it opened in 1973. Wharton said the $30,000 initiative funded only these two markers for now, but he hopes to secure more funding to add additional stories in the future.
item.dc:creator: Tim Vandenack, KSL

item.title: 'Moderate to severe' turbulence reported prior to fatal plane crash in Utah Lake
item.description: A newly released NTSB preliminary report found that multiple aircraft near Provo Municipal Airport reported moderate to severe turbulence shortly before an ATP Flight School training plane crashed into Utah Lake on Aug. 7, killing student pilot Chase Riley Day, 25, and seriously injuring his flight instructor. The Cessna 172 Skyhawk entered a rapid descent seconds after takeoff, and airport security cameras captured dust plumes moving through the area beforehand. The plane's cabin, engine and both wings were found submerged in Provo Bay within a roughly 100-foot debris field. The NTSB says its investigation into the crash's cause is continuing; Day was laid to rest on Aug. 15.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Provo mayor defends Vesper Amphitheater as Vivint founder, others express concerns
item.description: Provo Mayor Marsha Judkins urged residents to let the review process play out for the proposed 20,000-seat Vesper Amphitheater in Provo Canyon, an Osmond-family-backed project that also includes a 75-room hotel and extensive parking on land partly owned by the city. Developers recently withdrew their application to rework plans addressing concerns about traffic, noise and parking, and plan to resubmit by month's end. Vivint founder Todd Pedersen, an Orem resident near the canyon mouth, said he isn't opposed to development generally but is alarmed by the potential traffic impact, and the city of Orem has formally objected that the project's impacts are too significant to ignore. Judkins said she isn't committed to approval "at all costs" but believes exploring the proposal is the responsible course.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Waves of layoffs are sweeping across Utah. Here's what workers losing their jobs should know
item.description: Thousands of Utah workers have lost jobs in 2026 amid cutbacks at companies including Tyson Foods, Qualtrics, Crumbl and Sheraton, with Tyson laying off more than 700 employees at its Eagle Mountain plant as it shutters facilities amid a 75-year low in U.S. cattle supplies. Laid-off maintenance worker Austin Campbell said he's grateful for his degree but wary of relocating to another Tyson site given the industry's turmoil, and noted the company's above-market pay makes finding comparable wages elsewhere difficult. Nationally, job cuts are running 41% below last year's pace, the lowest January-through-August total since 2022, but hiring has also slowed to a "no hire, no fire" dynamic, according to Challenger, Gray & Christmas. The Utah Department of Workforce Services said it offers free assistance, including job-search help, for displaced workers navigating the transition.
item.dc:creator: Art Raymond, Deseret News

item.title: Competency evaluation ordered for man accused of setting Timp Fire
item.description: A 4th District Court judge ordered a mental competency evaluation for Conrad Jared Larsen, 46, who is charged with four counts of arson including the July 9 Timp Fire that forced evacuations near Timpooneke Campground. Larsen's defense attorney argued in her petition that he struggles to understand the charges against him, can't recall key details of the fires or conversations with counsel, and has described a "supernatural force" and hearing spirits he called "cursed." A letter from Larsen's brother cited a self-reported diagnosis of schizoid personality disorder and described him as estranged from family with rigid, altered thinking, though the brother said he doesn't view Larsen as malicious or violent. The Utah Department of Human Services has been ordered to arrange a forensic evaluation.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Crowds flock to Utah canyon areas to mark Labor Day
item.description: Hundreds of people packed Tibble Fork Reservoir in American Fork Canyon on Labor Day to paddleboard, swim and relax in mild, sunny weather. Visitors including Sabrina Longman and Kiersty Sutton, the latter visiting from Idaho with a group of students, praised the reservoir's scenery and atmosphere. South Jordan resident Chris Keller, who brought his family after a morning of four-wheeling and hiking, said the outing was a fun way to mark the end of summer before kids return to school. Several visitors expressed mixed feelings about summer ending, with some looking forward to Utah's fall colors.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: This Salt Lake City taco shop is looking to expand without losing unique 'alley street feel'
item.description: Five years after opening in a Salt Lake City alley, ROCTACO is looking to expand its globally inspired taco concept to more locations in Utah and potentially beyond, co-owner Rick Timmons told KSL. Timmons and his brother Ryan drew the menu's international flavors, including Korean bulgogi and Indian chicken tikka masala tacos, from their Church of Jesus Christ mission trips and Rick's two decades living in Asia, while resisting the "fusion" label. The brothers brought in culinary experts for each cuisine to ensure authenticity and spent a year and a half perfecting their made-from-scratch tortillas. Rick Timmons said the concept has proven itself enough to justify moving from a single location toward broader growth.
item.dc:creator: Logan Stefanich, KSL

item.title: 1 killed in crash on state Route 89 in Utah County
item.description: A passenger died Monday morning after a Honda Civic crossed double yellow lines to pass another vehicle near Birdseye and struck a southbound Toyota Tacoma head-on, according to the Utah Highway Patrol. The crash occurred around 10:30 a.m. on state Route 89, and both drivers were taken to nearby hospitals by ambulance. Authorities had not released additional details about the deceased passenger's identity as of the report.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: 'Remarkable' noses — new dogs in Utah corrections program can search for electronics
item.description: Utah's Adult Probation and Parole introduced two new K-9s, Glitch and Cypher, trained to sniff out phones, SD cards and other electronic storage devices hidden by people on probation or parole, particularly the roughly 1,700 sex offenders under internet-access restrictions among the more than 15,000 people the agency supervises. Officer Josh Paxman said Glitch found two hidden phones in 20 minutes at a home where other agents had searched unsuccessfully for 90 minutes. The dogs, donated by the nonprofit Defenders for Children, were trained in Indianapolis and have searched roughly 80 Utah residences combined since arriving, recovering phones, a drone and multiple smartwatches. Defenders for Children executive director Toni Clark said the dogs serve as a reminder to offenders that violations will send them back to prison.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Peteetneet Fire in Payson now 60% contained
item.description: The Peteetneet Fire burning near Nebo Loop Road in Payson reached 60% containment after crews worked through the night to secure its perimeter, according to Utah Division of Forestry, Fire and State Lands spokesperson Kayli Guild. The blaze, which grew to about 45 acres after starting Sunday, is being fought by both ground crews and aircraft, with no closures currently in place. Guild said a golf course separates the fire from nearby neighborhoods and that there have been no impacts to infrastructure or watersheds so far, though officials asked people to avoid the area. The fire's cause is confirmed as human-caused but remains under investigation.
item.dc:creator: Madi Vollmer, KSL

item.title: Driver killed early Sunday in rollover crash
item.description: A driver was killed early Sunday when a BMW went off westbound I-80 near 6200 West in Salt Lake City for unknown reasons and rolled down an embankment, according to the Utah Highway Patrol. Cashton Gamble, 19, of Heber City, was partially ejected and pronounced dead at the scene; a 21-year-old passenger was hospitalized in critical condition with multiple broken bones and head injuries. Neither occupant was wearing a seatbelt, and investigators are looking at speed and impairment as possible contributing factors.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Bicyclist hit, killed in Provo
item.description: A 63-year-old cyclist died after being struck by a vehicle exiting I-15 at the University Avenue off-ramp and Lakeview Parkway in Provo on Monday morning, police said. He was taken to Utah Valley Hospital but did not survive his injuries. Provo police said the driver is cooperating with the investigation and that impairment is not suspected, and the intersection reopened around midday.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Company believes drone cloud seeding tech could help restore the Great Salt Lake in the future
item.description: California-based Rainmaker Technology Corporation says its drone-based cloud seeding process produced 19 million gallons of precipitation over three hours in a recent Alaska test, and founder Augustus Doricko told KSL the company is partnering with the Utah Department of Natural Resources on plans to eventually apply the technology to help restore the shrinking Great Salt Lake. Doricko said Rainmaker uses radar, balloons, drones and satellites to identify clouds holding supercooled water droplets, then seeds them with dust so they grow into precipitation-sized flakes. Utah Division of Water Resources meteorologist Jonathan Jennings said the Alaska test built on 2017's SNOWIE research and that verified precipitation gains, even modest ones, could meaningfully ease stress on Utah's water supply over a decade or two. Doricko acknowledged critics' concerns about cumulative effects of cloud-seeding chemicals and said stronger federal regulation will likely be needed as the technology scales.
item.dc:creator: Andrew Adams, KSL

item.title: Holocaust survivor to speak at University of Utah
item.description: Sora Vigorito, the youngest known survivor of Nazi doctor Josef Mengele's twin experiments at Auschwitz, will speak at the University of Utah on Sept. 15, according to Rabbi Moshe Nigri of Chabad on Campus. Vigorito was 3 years old when she and her twin sister were taken to Auschwitz in 1944; her sister died in the camp, but Vigorito survived until its 1945 liberation. Nigri said Vigorito rarely travels to Utah given the state's small Jewish population, and organizers expect 150 to 200 attendees at the 7 p.m. event in the Gardner Commons' Siciliano Auditorium, co-sponsored by several campus interfaith groups. Nigri said the story carries a message relevant to people of any faith.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: From the beginning of the Edwards Era, Dave Hanna watched a leadership guru at work
item.description: Dave Hanna, who worked in BYU's sports information office as LaVell Edwards began his head coaching tenure in 1972, has written a new book, "LaVell's Leadership Playbook," drawing business leadership lessons from Edwards' coaching style. Hanna recalled Edwards being overcome with emotion after BYU's 1974 upset of 16th-ranked Arizona State, and said the moment reflected how deeply players respected Edwards' leadership. After a career at Procter & Gamble and as a corporate consultant, Hanna said he came to view Edwards as the equal of top business executives he'd studied, prompting him to identify eight leadership principles Edwards consistently applied. Hanna's book arrives the same month as a second book on Edwards, "The Leadership of LaVell Edwards" by Mark D. Ogletree and Dave McCann, underscoring the coach's enduring legacy a decade after his death.
item.dc:creator: Lee Benson, Deseret News

item.title: Utah data centers promise jobs and revenue, but opponents say benefits disappear
item.description: Utah residents and researchers are questioning whether promised economic benefits of new data centers, including lower electricity and property tax bills, actually materialize, according to reporting centered on Box Elder County activist Brenna Williams' opposition to the proposed Stratos data center. USC professor Shon Hiatt told a legislative interim committee that investor-owned utilities like Rocky Mountain Power haven't passed data-center costs to other customers so far, but warned that trend could change as larger facilities arrive, and that utilities without similar resources tend to raise rates instead. University of Utah public finance researcher Maddy Oritt described a "boomerang effect" in property taxes, where new data-center construction initially lowers other residents' rates by expanding the tax base, but the effect fades as the facilities' taxable equipment depreciates over time. The story notes Utah's Truth in Taxation system separates real property like buildings from personal property like servers, which is taxed differently as it ages.
item.dc:creator: Leah Bowers, Deseret News

item.title: Wildfire threatens structures in Payson
item.description: The Peteetneet Fire, burning near Nebo Loop Road in Payson, grew to roughly 45 acres and was threatening nearby structures as of Sunday night, when it was 0% contained, according to Utah Fire Info. Firefighters battled the blaze from the air and ground, with a golf course roughly half a mile wide serving as a buffer between the fire and nearby homes, Payson Fire Department spokesperson Scott Spencer said. Utah Fire Info asked residents to avoid the area to give firefighters room to work safely.
item.dc:creator: Kennedy Camarena, KSL

item.title: Pineview draw down brings rare low levels, slump in activity
item.description: Crowds at Pineview Reservoir near Huntsville were unusually thin heading into Labor Day weekend as Ogden City crews draw down the lake to replace a 1970s-era 36-inch water pipeline serving about 120,000 people. Water levels have fallen to roughly 17% of normal and are expected to dip to near 2% of normal, or about 2,000 acre-feet, by mid-September, the lowest since the original pipeline was installed, according to the Weber Basin Water Conservancy District. Anglers Sam Fortney and Kameron Mickelson, the latter having driven from Mesquite, Nevada, in hopes of catching tiger muskies concentrated in the shrinking lake, both remarked on how strange the low water looked. Club Rec co-owner Paul Avner said business has slowed at the reservoir's Cemetery Point location, which will move to reservations-only after Labor Day, while the company's Willard Bay site remains busy.
item.dc:creator: Mike Anderson, KSL

item.title: 22-year-old Kaysville woman with Down syndrome becomes certified fitness instructor
item.description: Aubry Alldredge, 22, of Kaysville became the first person with Down syndrome to earn certification as a UpBeat Barre instructor at VASA Fitness after years of attending classes there. She recently taught her first class to more than 60 people and says she loves motivating others and helping everyone feel included. Co-owner and instructor Jane Johnson praised Alldredge's quick grasp of choreography and stage presence, and said the gym hopes to bring her on as an official instructor. Alldredge also co-wrote a children's book with her sisters, called "I Have a Six Pack," inspired by the six rescue dogs she cares for, meant to promote inclusion for people with Down syndrome.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Spanish Fork woman to serve year in prison for cyberstalking, harassing 2 victims
item.description: A federal judge sentenced Kailin Wang, 43, of Spanish Fork to a year in prison and three years of probation after she pleaded guilty to cyberstalking two men she met on dating sites in California starting in 2017 and 2018. Prosecutors said Wang waged years-long harassment campaigns against the men and their families, including defamatory online posts, false reports to law enforcement and the FBI's internet crimes unit, and threats against one victim. She also pleaded guilty in Utah state court to a false statement and forgery charge for using misleading evidence to seek a protective order against one of the men. Prosecutors noted Wang had a prior 2013 stalking conviction in New York, and her probation now bars her from contacting the victims or their families and requires her to disclose the conviction to future partners.
item.dc:creator: Cassidy Wixom, KSL

item.title: 'Trackflation' is here: Why Utah's young runners are getting so fast
item.description: KSL profiled the rise of unusually fast youth running times in Utah, a trend coaches call "trackflation," centered on 13-year-old Provo runner Angelina Alder, whose 4:38.25 mile this summer set an age-group world record. Roadrunner Junior Club founder John Hedengren, a former BYU All-American runner who now teaches chemical engineering, said times that were nationally elite a generation ago no longer crack the top 100. He attributed the shift to wider access to elite training knowledge, better nutrition and coaching, "super shoes" with carbon plates that measurably improve running efficiency for some athletes, and Utah County's altitude, which can boost endurance at lower elevations. Hedengren's club has grown from 17 athletes in 2019 to more than 180 today, and he said watching peers like Alder succeed inspires other young runners to push their own limits.
item.dc:creator: Eric Cabrera, KSL

item.title: $1.2M donation to UNICEF from Church of Jesus Christ to care for moms, babies in Pakistan
item.description: The Church of Jesus Christ of Latter-day Saints announced a two-year, $1.2 million collaboration with UNICEF to improve maternal and newborn care for about 410,000 mothers in Pakistan, part of a broader initiative aimed at 1.5 million mothers across South Asia. Relief Society General President Camille N. Johnson said the effort aims to close care gaps around childbirth, while UNICEF officials Pernille Ironside and Sanjay Wijesekera said the funding will help prevent some of the roughly 700 newborn deaths and two maternal deaths Pakistan sees each day. Elder Kelly R. Johnson, the church's Asia Area president, said the goal is to extend life-saving care to more mothers and infants in the region. The funding will go toward supplies, health-worker training and improved data systems to help identify high-risk pregnancies.
item.dc:creator: Emily Ashcraft, KSL

item.title: Developers 'hit pause' on Vesper Amphitheater plans after public pushback
item.description: Developers behind the Osmond family's proposed 20,000-seat Vesper Amphitheater in Provo Canyon withdrew their application to Provo City after strong public opposition, including a formal letter of concern this week from neighboring Orem over noise, traffic and impacts on Mount Timpanogos Park. Vesper representative Bryan Bayles told KSL developers plan to resubmit a revised application by month's end that shrinks retail and restaurant space to 40,000 square feet while keeping the venue's 20,000-seat capacity and a planned 75-room hotel. Orem officials, including council member Crystal Muhlestein, remain skeptical any revision can resolve concerns about commercializing the canyon, while Provo council member Travis Hoban said he remains undecided after touring the site. Executive director David Osmond said the developers are Utah natives who understand the area's sensitivity and are working to address public feedback.
item.dc:creator: Daniel Woodruff, KSL

item.title: Advice for Utah homebuyers as rates near previous highs
item.description: A global sell-off in government bonds this week pushed U.S. mortgage rates toward 7% for the first time since January 2025, with Freddie Mac's 30-year fixed average climbing to 6.71% and some lenders quoting even higher. Economists including First American's Mark Fleming and reporting from The Wall Street Journal linked the rise to 10-year Treasury yields hitting a three-year high amid concerns over the ongoing U.S.-Israel war against Iran and a national debt topping $40 trillion. Zions Bank Mortgage's Jeremy Holmgren said the psychological impact of a 7% rate outweighs its practical difference from 6.75%, and urged buyers to focus on today's affordability rather than trying to time the market. He added that buyers who don't wait on the sidelines may benefit from less competition and more leverage with sellers as Utah's housing inventory continues to grow.
item.dc:creator: Lisa Riley Roche, Deseret News

item.title: Moroni Elementary educator Talia Casares named Utah's 2027 'Teacher of the Year'
item.description: Utah's State Board of Education named Talia Casares, a sixth-grade Spanish dual-language immersion teacher at Moroni Elementary in the North Sanpete School District, as the state's 2027 Teacher of the Year. Casares, originally from Mexico City and a BYU master's graduate who researched literacy and STEM integration in dual-language classrooms, was chosen from five finalists by a committee of state board, advocacy, higher-education and charter-school representatives. She has taught for nine years and previously won the 2025 Utah Coalition for Educational Technology's Innovative Teacher Award. Casares receives $10,000 and will represent Utah in a national teacher-of-the-year competition next year, while the four other finalists each received $2,000.

item.title: How one woman's grief turned into a yearslong mission to prevent suicide
item.description: Salt Lake County tax lien coordinator Ray Lancaster, whose adult son died by suicide in 2017, spent eight years pushing the county to formally recognize September as Suicide Prevention and Awareness Month, finally succeeding this week with help from County Treasurer Sheila Srivastava, whose teenage son survived a mental health crisis after witnessing his father's fatal heart attack. Mayor Jenny Wilson and the County Council signed a proclamation Tuesday urging residents to learn warning signs, check on struggling loved ones, and share the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline, while inviting the public to Saturday's Out of the Darkness Community Walk in West Jordan. Wilson grew emotional recounting the recent death of Colin Hilton, the former Utah Olympic Legacy Foundation president. Lancaster and Srivastava said sharing their stories has helped them find community, and both plan to keep advocating for awareness beyond this year's proclamation.
item.dc:creator: Bridger Beal-Cvetko, KSL

item.title: Utah mother of young twins accused by federal grand jury of abuse
item.description: A federal grand jury indicted Fayette Whitehorse, 27, of Aneth on two counts of aggravated child abuse in Indian country after her 3-month-old twins were airlifted from Blanding to Primary Children's Hospital on Aug. 24 with multiple fractures and, in the boy's case, a brain hemorrhage. Whitehorse was arrested Aug. 26 following an FBI interview in which, according to charging documents, she admitted causing several of the injuries out of frustration while caring for the infants. The twins, born prematurely in May, had fractures in different stages of healing, indicating repeated incidents over time. The case remains pending in federal court following the indictment.
item.dc:creator: Pat Reavy, KSL

item.title: Historic Dixie Sunbowl gets major upgrades, increases capacity
item.description: St. George's nearly 80-year-old Dixie Sunbowl stadium completed a roughly $3.7 million renovation, funded by a voter-approved bond and Washington County RAP tax funds, that replaced its aging concrete bleachers and boosted capacity by about 1,000 seats to 7,300. Contractor Gene Madsen of Hughes General Contractors said crews demolished and rebuilt the venue in about a year after last year's rodeo to address safety and comfort issues the deteriorating 1947 stadium could no longer support. Madsen said the venue, originally built through community donations and Lions Club labor, remains deeply meaningful to St. George residents. The Sunbowl holds its grand reopening Sept. 10, just ahead of the Dixie Round-up Rodeo running Sept. 17-19.
item.dc:creator: Arianne Brown, KSL

item.title: Fire in Washington County burns multiple homes
item.description: A fire broke out Friday afternoon near Wagon Wheel Drive and Cottonmill East Avenue in Washington City, sending black smoke over the community and destroying or damaging multiple homes and vehicles. Battalion Chief Brandon Moore said the blaze started in one building before spreading to a shed used to store live ammunition, which ignited and forced crews to briefly retreat for safety before two more structures caught fire amid windy conditions. Neighbor Lani Lawrence, whose own home burned down in 2013, said she feared history was repeating when she saw the smoke while driving home from a grocery store. Fire crews expected the response to stretch for hours as they worked to fully extinguish the blaze.
item.dc:creator: Joe R. Wirthlin Jr, KSL

item.title: Afro Utah Festival returns, highlighting the mix of cultures in Utah rooted in Africa
item.description: The Afro Utah Festival returns for its sixth year Saturday to Salt Lake City's Main Library plaza, offering free food, entertainment, crafts and business booths celebrating Afro Caribbean, African American, Afro Latino and African cultures. Organizer Gloria Mensah of the GK Folks Foundation, originally from Nigeria, said the event began in 2021 to support Black-owned businesses hurt by the pandemic and has since grown to draw upward of 5,000 attendees. This year's festival runs noon to 9 p.m. and is headlined by Virgin Islands soca artist Pumpa, with a stretch of 200 East closing for the event. A companion Afro Utah Awards ceremony Friday recognized community members for their achievements ahead of Saturday's festivities.
